description: Abdullah (Grade 9) and Aws (Grade 8). Green Space Autonomous Farm is a smart ESP32 farm sensing temperature, humidity, CO2, NH3, soil moisture and water level. Space → Earth: we compare our sensors with NASA POWER and SMAP data to water smarter. Earth → Space: the same kit, adapted for astronauts to grow food and turn waste into compost. Our prototype won Best Idea at Jordan's National Innovation & Robotics Championship 2025.
summary:
We developed Green Space Autonomous Farm, a low-cost smart farm that works in two directions: Space → Earth and Earth → Space.

What we built: an ESP32 kit with sensors for air temperature and humidity (DHT22), CO2 (MQ-135), ammonia NH3 (MQ-137), soil moisture and water level. It shows live readings on a web dashboard, waters plants automatically, and monitors a compost unit that turns food and plant scraps into fertilizer.

How it addresses Field Shift: we connect the farm to NASA POWER and SMAP data for the farm's location. The app compares our ground sensors with NASA's temperature, humidity, rainfall and soil-wetness data, checks sensor accuracy, and gives simple alerts: skip watering before rain, water when soil is dry, warn about heat stress, and suggest crops for the season and climate.

Why it matters: climate change makes farming harder, especially in dry regions like Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Our kit helps anyone, even non-experts, save water and grow food. The same closed-loop kit can go to space, helping astronauts grow fresh food, monitor a sealed cabin, and recycle waste into compost.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Green Space Autonomous Farm is a low-cost smart farm that works in two directions:
- Space → Earth: our farm uses NASA POWER data for its exact location to make better decisions on Earth.
- Earth → Space: the same kit is designed as a grow package for astronauts on long missions.

HOW IT WORKS
- Hardware: an ESP32 microcontroller reads six sensors: air temperature and humidity (DHT22), CO2 / air quality (MQ-135), ammonia NH3 (MQ-137), soil moisture, and water level (dry / wet / water). It controls a water pump automatically and serves the readings over Wi-Fi.
- NASA data: our web app downloads daily NASA POWER data for the farm's coordinates: air temperature (T2M), humidity (RH2M), rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), solar radiation, wind and surface soil wetness (GWETTOP).
- Compare and act: the app compares our ground sensors with NASA's regional data to check sensor accuracy, and gives simple alerts: skip watering when rain is expected, water when the soil is dry, heat-stress warnings, compost status from NH3, and crops to plant for the season and climate.
- Compost: a compost unit turns food and plant scraps into fertilizer. The NH3 and CO2 sensors show when the compost is active, too strong, or ready.

SPACE VERSION
In space, plants grow inside a sealed chamber. Our kit monitors CO2 and NH3 build-up that a closed cabin cannot vent, measures every drop of water in a closed loop, and recycles crew food scraps and inedible plant parts into compost. The astronaut chooses their habitat (ISS, Moon base, Mars), and the app shows outside conditions such as day/night cycles and space weather.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
- Saves water in dry regions like Jordan and Saudi Arabia, where climate change makes farming harder.
- Simple enough for non-experts, such as a mother growing vegetables at home, and for any crew member in space.
- Low cost, built from common parts, and easy to copy.
- Reduces waste by turning scraps into fertilizer, on Earth and in space.

TOOLS
ESP32 (Arduino IDE, C++), DHT22, MQ-135, MQ-137, soil moisture and water level sensors, a water pump, Next.js / React / TypeScript for the web app, the NASA POWER API, OpenStreetMap, and Python for data comparison. AI tools (Claude and OpenAI Codex) helped us write texts, make the demo video and build the website; we reviewed and adapted everything.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
One kit, two worlds: the same farm helps families on Earth using data from space, and goes to space to help astronauts grow food.

BEFORE AND DURING THE HACKATHON
Our hardware prototype was built and tested before the hackathon, and won Best Idea at Jordan's National Innovation & Robotics Championship 2025. During this hackathon we connected it to NASA data, built the comparison and alerts, and designed the astronaut version.

Team: Abdullah Ashraf Al-Naasan (Grade 9) and Aws Ashraf Al-Naasan (Grade 8). Mentored by our science teacher, Ms. Esraa Thamneh.
